Paper_name: Towards The Boundaries of Self-Prioritization: Associating The Self With Asymmetric Shapes Disrupts The Self-Prioritization Effect
Summary: The study investigates whether a salient perceptual feature—symmetry—can modulate the self-prioritization effect, where self-relevant information is processed more efficiently than other-relevant information. Participants associated the self with either symmetric or asymmetric shapes and a stranger with the opposite shape type in a matching task. A clear self-prioritization effect emerged when the self was linked to symmetric shapes, but no effect was observed when the self was linked to asymmetric shapes. The results indicate that self-prioritization is not mandatory and can be disrupted by associating the self with negatively valenced stimuli like asymmetry.
Author: Michele Vicovaro, Mario Dalmaso, Marco Bertamini
Journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
Conclusion: The self-prioritization effect is not automatic and can be modulated by stimulus valence. Associating the self with asymmetric (negatively valenced) shapes completely disrupts the effect, whereas associating the self with symmetric shapes preserves it. This demonstrates that perceptual and evaluative properties of stimuli interact with self-association to influence cognitive prioritization.
